content: The mitochondrial lineages found in Africa are among the most ancient and diverse in the world. This suggests that Africa had a longer period to accumulate genetic mutations compared to other regions. In evolutionary biology, the area with the greatest genetic diversity is often considered the place of origin for a species. Using this principle, scientists reconstructed the genetic relationships between various mitochondrial haplogroups and created a phylogenetic tree. They discovered that all African and non-African mitochondrial lineages converge on a single common ancestor, termed Mitochondrial Eve. This ancestor represents the most recent common maternal lineage of all humans alive today. Further analysis identified a specific African mitochondrial lineage, haplogroup L3e, as the root of all mitochondrial lineages found outside Africa. This evidence supports the hypothesis that the human species originated from a single genetic lineage in Africa within the last 200,000 years, rather than multiple lineages arising independently in different locations. Mitochondrial Eve was not the only woman alive at the time, but her lineage is the only one that has persisted unbroken to the present day. Some researchers propose that humanity faced a near-extinction event within the last 100,000 years, possibly due to a catastrophic event like the Toba volcanic eruption. This bottleneck may have reduced the human population to as few as 2,000 individuals, leading to the extinction of other maternal lineages and leaving only Eve's lineage to dominate. This phenomenon is known as the founder effect. It is widely accepted that modern humans first emerged in Africa and later migrated to colonize Eurasia and other parts of the world. However, the exact timing and routes of these migrations remain subjects of debate. Due to the complexity of migration patterns over time, scientists continue to revise and refine theories as new evidence emerges. The first mitochondrial lineage to diverge from Mitochondrial Eve is haplogroup L1, which is found in high frequencies among the San and Mbuti peoples. These groups split off early in human history and have remained relatively genetically isolated. Haplogroups L2 and L3, descendants of L1, are primarily confined to Africa. Outside Africa, the major haplogroups M and N, which are descendants of L3, represent the mitochondrial lineages of the rest of the world. Some scientists suggest that only a small group of humans left Africa in a single migration event, which eventually populated the rest of the world. It is estimated that from a population of 2,000–5,000 individuals in Africa, a small group of approximately 150 people crossed the Red Sea. This is supported by the observation that only the descendants of one African lineage, L3, are found outside Africa. If multiple migrations had occurred, more than one African lineage would be expected to appear outside the continent. The daughters of L3, haplogroups M and N, are found in very low frequencies in Africa and appear to have emerged shortly before or after the exodus from Africa. The founder effect likely played a role in their dominance outside Africa. An alternative hypothesis suggests two separate migrations out of Africa. One group, associated with haplogroup M, traveled along coastal routes from the Red Sea to India. Another group, associated with haplogroup N, followed the Nile River northward and crossed into Asia via the Sinai Peninsula. This second group then branched in multiple directions, with some moving into Europe and others heading east into Asia. This theory attempts to explain why haplogroup N is predominant in Europe, while haplogroup M is absent there. The coastal group associated with haplogroup M appears to have settled first in India, where it exhibits the greatest genetic diversity. Haplogroup M is found in high frequencies along the southern coastal regions of Pakistan and India, with 60% of the Indian population belonging to this lineage. Indigenous populations of the Andaman Islands also belong to haplogroup M, suggesting they are remnants of some of the earliest settlers in Asia due to their long genetic isolation from mainland populations. The Andamanese provide evidence of the coastal migration route that extended from India along the coasts of Thailand and Indonesia to Papua New Guinea. Haplogroup M is also found in high frequencies among highlanders in New Guinea. The physical characteristics of the Andamanese and New Guineans, such as dark skin and frizzy hair, resemble those of Africans, leading some scientists to propose that they are part of the same wave of migrants who crossed the Red Sea. Others argue that these similarities are more likely due to convergent evolution. From Saudi Arabia to India, the proportion of haplogroup M increases eastward, with M outnumbering N by a ratio of 3:1 in eastern India. However, in East Asia, haplogroup N reemerges as the dominant lineage. Haplogroup M is predominant in Southeast Asia, but among Indigenous Australians, haplogroup N becomes more common. This discontinuous distribution of haplogroup N from Europe to Australia has puzzled scientists attempting to trace migratory routes. Both haplogroups M and N have descendants found in the Americas. Regarding physical appearance, there is significant speculation about the characteristics of ancient Homo sapiens during the time of Mitochondrial Eve and prior to their exodus from Africa. Some scientists theorize that all modern human physical variation originated from this small African population. Hairlessness is an uncommon trait among mammals, but humans, along with aquatic mammals like dolphins and hippopotamuses, and the naked mole rat, have lost much of their body hair. Most non-human primates have lightly pigmented skin covered by fur. Early protohominids likely resembled chimpanzees, with white skin covered by dark hair. As hominids began walking upright and moved from forested areas to open savannahs, they required more efficient cooling systems. The human brain, which consumes significant energy, is highly sensitive to heat, necessitating advanced thermoregulation. Humans evolved more sweat glands, particularly on the face, which required the loss of body hair to facilitate effective evaporation. Sexual selection may have also played a role in favoring hairless skin. While hairless skin aids in thermoregulation, it exposes the epidermis to harmful ultraviolet (UV) radiation, which can cause sunburn, skin cancer, and folate destruction, leading to birth defects. To protect against UV damage, natural selection favored increased melanin levels in the skin. Consequently, the first modern humans are believed to have been dark-skinned. As humans migrated to regions with less intense sunlight, the dark skin adapted for blocking UV radiation in the tropics became a disadvantage, as it hindered the production of vitamin D, essential for bone growth. Deficiencies in vitamin D can lead to rickets. In these less sun-intensive regions, skin color lightened to allow sufficient UV radiation for vitamin D synthesis, but this occurred without the reemergence of body hair.
